articles.title_orig: Spain agrees on measures to fix housing crisis, ban eviction
articles.title_zh: Spain agrees on measures to fix housing crisis, ban eviction
articles.content_orig:
Spain's coalition government on Tuesday said it has agreed new measures to tackle the country's housing crisis after the forceful removal of an 87-year-old pensioner from her apartment in Madrid last week, sparked nationwide solidarity protests.
Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia said the housing legislation includes a ban on evictions until 2030, tighter rules for short-term rentals and a two-year extension for existing leases.
"It's ‌time ​to intervene in the speculative housing market and ​begin to rebalance the scales between ⁠citizens ​and vulture funds," ​Garcia, who belongs ​to the ‌leftist government's junior coalition partner Sumar, ​wrote ⁠in a post on ⁠X.
The Spanish government, led by Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and his ministers, approved the measures after a meeting.
But since Sanchez leads a minority government, he is still dependent on votes from a number of other parties in parliament before the bill is set in law.
Sanchez's ruling Socialists were engaged in talks with coalition partners Sumar and others up to Tuesday.
Socialist Housing Minister Isabel Rodriguez is scheduled to address a press conference later on Tuesday.
Images and videos last week that showed Maria del Carmen Abascal — known by her nickname Maricarmen — escorted out of her apartment by riot police officers touched a nerve among Spaniards who've long called for a solution to the housing crisis in the country.
Maricarmen's father had first rented the property in 1956 in Madrid's Retiro neighborhood and she continued as the tenant after her parents died.
Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Maricarmen had rented the apartment from a private landlord until 2018, after which a real estate company acquired the property and took over its management.
According to the newspaper, the legal dispute between Maricarmen and the real estate company lasted eight years and their latest attempt to evict her from the apartment marked their fourth attempt to do so.
The issue placed Spain's housing market in the spotlight where many long-term tenants have been priced out of their apartments due to an affordability crisis and a shortage of homes in Europe's fourth-largest economy.
Protesters rallied around Maricarmen's cause, especially because pictures of her being taken out of her apartment building and into an ambulance were vividly present across social media.
She is a wheelchair user too.
People then hit the streets of Madrid in the thousands on Saturday, with many having ended their protest by setting up tents in Madrid's historic Puerta del Sol plaza at the end of the night.
More people, including multigenerational families, joined Sunday.
Maricarmen's lawyer on Monday said that she was going to be able to return home, calling the victory a "result of the social mobilization."
"If this agreement we have reached is signed, it will obviously be a better and happier outcome for everyone," Abascal's lawyer Beatriz Duro told reporters.
"Hopefully this agreement, this different way of ending this type of situation, which is unfortunately experienced every day in this country, helps to change the paradigm when it comes to housing in general," Duro said.

Goldman Sachs ( GS ) CEO David Solomon just got the clearest public indication yet of when his long-anticipated successor, No. 2 executive John Waldron, could replace him atop the storied Wall Street bank.
Goldman's board has discussed a plan for Solomon to step down as CEO as soon as the end of 2027 or 2028, according to a Wall Street Journal report from late Monday that cited unnamed sources, potentially putting a timetable around the leadership change that the bank has been preparing for publicly for years.
Board approval of the plan would need to take place in the coming months, according to the report.
"Of course the Board regularly discusses succession, as we disclose in our filings," a Goldman spokesperson, Tony Fratto, said in an emailed statement to Yahoo Finance.
"But there is no definitive timeline for succession at Goldman Sachs," Fratto added, calling any assertions about timing speculative.
Following the report, Goldman's stock rose slightly in after-market trading. It's up more than 4% for the year.
The plan would line up the timeline for an end to Solomon's tenure with Goldman firmly back on offense. Since Solomon officially became CEO eight years ago, Goldman's stock has quadrupled to $916 per share as of Monday's closing price.
So far this year, Solomon has presided over a heyday for Goldman's core Wall Street machine. AI-driven capital raising, a boom in corporate mergers, and this year's unusually active markets have all accelerated the growth of its core trading and dealmaking franchises.
As recently as July, Solomon, who turns 65 in January, acknowledged that a transition would eventually come while pushing back on the idea that it was imminent.
"I'm really excited about the firm and what the firm can accomplish over the course of the next three to five years," he said when asked about succession in an interview with CNBC's David Faber.
"At some point in time, there'll be a transition, but it's not now," Solomon said.
His tenure has also been far from free of speed bumps, which is nothing new for Goldman leadership .
Five years into the job in 2023, Solomon faced mounting pressure as he steered the company through its most challenging year of the last decade. In the summer of that year, Goldman reported its lowest quarterly profits in three years as senior management wrestled with everything from job cuts and a dealmaking slump to reports of partner unrest and a tricky retreat from an ill-fated attempt at consumer banking.
Waldron, who is 57, joined Goldman a year after Solomon and was known as a career investment banker. He became chief operating officer in October 2018.
His position as a successor candidate became increasingly apparent following that rocky period, as a number of high-profile executives exited , and even Goldman's board of directors changed.
Last year, he received a five-year retention bonus from the board, then valued at $80 million, alongside Solomon, with Goldman explicitly citing the goal to maintain "a strong succession plan for the future of the firm."

articles.title_orig: Terminally ill child euthanised in the Netherlands was one year old, government says
articles.title_zh: Terminally ill child euthanised in the Netherlands was one year old, government says
articles.content_orig:
The first terminally ill child to be euthanised in the Netherlands under an expansion of the country’s assisted-dying laws was one year old and is the youngest person in the world to die by euthanasia.
Dutch officials revealed in June that a child had died by euthanasia last year but gave no further details about the age of the infant or the terminal illness.
But an official government report published earlier this month said that the child had been born prematurely, had contracted sepsis and had been diagnosed with “extensive brain damage” at just four months.
The child was also diagnosed with a severe form of cerebral palsy and was later found to have a severe form of epilepsy.
“The child had sputum clearance problems, which means that it was difficult to loosen and cough up mucus from the lungs and airways. Besides shortness of breath, this leads to a considerably higher risk of respiratory infections,” the report said.
“In the course of the child’s short life, there was a complete lack of development or improvement.”
The report adds that the parents asked the child’s physician “to terminate the child’s life” when it became clear there was no hope of improvement.
The Netherlands legalised euthanasia for severely ill children between the ages of one and 12 in 2024.
Earlier this week, Dutch media reported that the Public Prosecution Service said it would not prosecute the doctor following advice from a committee that ruled earlier this month that the physician acted with due care.
"As a doctor, you are in an extremely vulnerable position, because this has never happened before. It still feels as if a sword of Damocles has been hanging over your head for almost a year," he said.
The Netherlands was the first country in the world to legalise euthanasia under strict conditions in 2002.
All cases must be reported to medical review boards.
Last year, 10,341 deaths by assisted suicide or euthanasia were reported in the Netherlands, according to the Regional Euthanasia Review Committees , representing a rise of 3.8% compared to 2024.
